e.meaning: God's people, or God is my kinsman
e.etymology: A Biblical Hebrew name joining El, God, and am, people or kinsman. In 2 Samuel, Eliam is the father of Bathsheba and one of David's warriors.
From French Stéphanie, the feminine form of Stephen, from Greek stephanos, crown or wreath. It was a top-ten American girls' name in the 1970s and 1980s.
namesakes: Stephanie Tanner (the middle sister on Full House)
Stephanie Beatriz (actress, Brooklyn Nine-Nine and Encanto)

e.etymology: A feminine form of Leon and Leo, from Latin leo, lion. It was most popular in the US in the early 1900s.
namesakes: Leona Helmsley (New York hotel magnate dubbed the Queen of Mean)
Leona Lewis (British singer, Bleeding Love)

e.etymology: A spelling of Jayden, a modern American name built on Jay and the -den ending it shares with Aiden, Brayden and Caden.
Madeline respelled with a -lynn ending. Madeline is the English form of French Madeleine, from Magdalene, woman of Magdala, a town on the Sea of Galilee whose name means tower.
The feminine form of the Latin saint's name Renatus, from renatus, reborn. French Renée is the same name.
A K spelling of Cora, tied to Greek kore, maiden, a title of Persephone. James Fenimore Cooper brought Cora into American use with The Last of the Mohicans in 1826.

assoc.t: Korra, heroine of The Legend of Korra (spelled Korra)
kora, a West African stringed instrument

e.etymology: A spelling of Caden, a modern American name that rose in the 2000s alongside rhyming names such as Aiden, Jayden and Brayden.
The Spanish and Portuguese form of Marcellus, a Roman pet form of Marcus, a name usually tied to Mars, the god of war.
From the surname and place name. Holland in the Netherlands comes from Old Dutch holt lant, wooded land; the English places called Holland are usually read as land by a hill spur.
namesakes: Holland Taylor (actress, Two and a Half Men)

assoc.t: Holland, the common name for the Netherlands
Tom Holland, the Spider-Man actor
Holland, Michigan, home of the Tulip Time festival

e.etymology: The Spanish and Portuguese form of Mark, from the Roman name Marcus, probably derived from Mars, the god of war. Saint Mark is the traditional author of the second Gospel.

assoc.t: Ferdinand Marcos and family, Philippine political dynasty

e.etymology: A Danish short form of Marina, from Latin marinus, of the sea, and also used in Denmark as a form of Maria.
namesakes: Maren Morris (country-pop singer)

e.etymology: From the English word halo, the ring of light shown around a holy figure's head, from Greek halos. It is a recent word name.

assoc.t: Halo, Xbox sci-fi shooter video game series
Halo, Beyonce's hit ballad
Halos, seedless mandarin oranges

e.etymology: The Italian form of Valentine, from Latin Valentinus, built on valens, strong or healthy. Saint Valentine and silent film star Rudolph Valentino both color the name.
namesakes: Valentino Garavani (Italian fashion designer known as Valentino)
Rudolph Valentino (silent film star)

assoc.t: Valentino, Italian luxury fashion house

e.etymology: From the English surname for someone who lived near a ford, a shallow place to cross a river. It is also the last syllable of names such as Clifford and Stanford.

assoc.t: Ford Motor Company, the car and truck maker
Henry Ford, Harrison Ford and President Gerald Ford

e.etymology: A short form of Alexa, Alexandra, Alexis and Alexia, names from the Greek root alexein, to defend.
From Greek Philippos, joining philein, to love, and hippos, horse. It was the name of kings of Macedon, including the father of Alexander the Great, and of one of the twelve apostles.
namesakes: Prince Philip (Duke of Edinburgh, husband of Queen Elizabeth II)
Philip Seymour Hoffman (Oscar-winning actor)
Philip Roth (novelist)

e.etymology: A short form of Mackenzie and other Mac- and Mc- surnames, where Gaelic mac means son, and sometimes of Max. It was most common as a given name in the late 1800s.

assoc.t: Mack Trucks, heavy truck maker with a bulldog logo
Mack, Lightning McQueen's hauler in Pixar's Cars
Mack the Knife, Bobby Darin's hit song
mack, slang for flirting with someone

e.etymology: The Italian form of the name of Saint Roch, a 14th-century French saint invoked against plague. The name is Germanic but its meaning is obscure; rest, crow and roar have all been suggested.
namesakes: Rocco DiSpirito (celebrity chef)

e.etymology: The English form of German Konrad, from Germanic words for bold and counsel.
namesakes: Conrad Hilton (founder of Hilton Hotels)
Conrad Fisher (love interest in The Summer I Turned Pretty)

assoc.t: Conrad Fisher of The Summer I Turned Pretty
Conrad Hotels & Resorts, Hilton's luxury brand

e.etymology: From Old English Eadgyth, joining ead, wealth or fortune, and gyth, strife. It was the name of a 10th-century English saint.
namesakes: Edith Wharton (novelist, The Age of Innocence)
Edith Piaf (French singer)
Edith Bunker (the wife on All in the Family)

e.etymology: The feminine of Fernando, the Spanish and Portuguese form of Ferdinand, a Germanic name usually read as bold journey.
From a surname for someone from Annesley in Nottinghamshire or Ansley in Warwickshire, place names joining Old English words for solitary or hermitage with leah, woodland clearing.
A name used widely by South Asian families, both Muslim and Hindu. It is usually glossed as gift of God, and some link it to Sanskrit ayana, path, but its derivation is not settled.
From French Élodie, a form of Alodia, the name of a 9th-century Spanish child martyr. Alodia is possibly a Gothic name whose second element means wealth or heritage.
An English spelling of Danish Søren, the medieval everyday form of Latin Severinus, from severus, stern or serious. Philosopher Søren Kierkegaard is its best-known bearer.
namesakes: Søren Kierkegaard (Danish philosopher)

e.meaning: the month of May; pet form of Mary or Margaret
e.etymology: A spelling of May, the month named for the Roman goddess Maia, and a pet form of Mary and Margaret. A favorite around 1900, it remains a popular middle name.
namesakes: Mae West (actress and wit)
Mae Jemison (first Black woman in space)
Mae Whitman (actress)

e.etymology: A single-m spelling of Emmanuel, from Hebrew Immanu'el, God is with us. The name comes from Isaiah's prophecy and is applied to Jesus in the Gospel of Matthew.
From the English word royalty. It became an American girls' name in the 2010s; singer Chris Brown named his daughter Royalty in 2014 and titled a 2015 album after her.

assoc.t: royalty, the word for kings, queens and their families

e.meaning: from a medieval Basque name, probably meaning son
e.etymology: The feminine of Jimeno, from Old Spanish Ximen and the Basque personal name Semen, likely from seme, son. Jimena Díaz was the wife of the Spanish hero El Cid. Ximena is the older spelling.
e.note: The Spanish J sounds like an English H; people who have not met the name may say jih-MEE-nuh.

e.meaning: lion (Hebrew); also a spelling of Aria, song
e.etymology: Used in two ways: as a spelling of Aria, the Italian musical term for a solo song, and as a form of Hebrew Aryeh, lion.
From French Florence and Latin Florentia, from florens, flowering or flourishing. Florence Nightingale, named for the Italian city where she was born, made it a 19th-century favorite.
namesakes: Florence Nightingale (founder of modern nursing)
Florence Pugh (actress, Little Women and Oppenheimer)
Florence Welch (singer of Florence and the Machine)

assoc.t: Florence, Italy, Renaissance city in Tuscany
Florence and the Machine, British rock band
Florence Nightingale, founder of modern nursing
Hurricane Florence, which flooded the Carolinas in 2018
